details:
**The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa**
Bernini's most famous work and the near-universal giveaway, made for the Cornaro Chapel in Rome's Santa Maria della Vittoria. It shows the Spanish Carmelite nun Teresa of Ávila swooning on a cloud while a smiling angel (sometimes called a cherub or Cupid-like figure) holds a golden arrow or spear aimed at her heart, a scene from her own account of a mystical vision.

**Cornaro Chapel**
The chapel housing The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, commissioned by Cardinal Federico Cornaro. Bernini staged it like a theater: a hidden window above lights the sculpture, gilded rays of light stream down behind Teresa, and marble members of the Cornaro family sit in balcony-like boxes on the side walls, watching the event.

**Fountain of the Four Rivers (Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi)**
Bernini's fountain in Rome's Piazza Navona, built for Pope Innocent X. Four river gods represent the Nile, Danube, Ganges, and Río de la Plata, one for each continent then known, seated around a rocky base that supports an Egyptian obelisk. A legend says one river god shields himself in fear that the facade of the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone (by his rival Borromini) will collapse, though the fountain was finished before that facade.

**Pamphili dove atop the obelisk**
A bronze dove holding an olive branch crowns the obelisk of the Fountain of the Four Rivers. It is the heraldic emblem of the Pamphili family of Pope Innocent X, whose family palace faces Piazza Navona.

**The Rape of Proserpina**
An early marble group made for Cardinal Scipione Borghese and now in the Galleria Borghese. Pluto (Hades) carries off Proserpina, whose hand pushes against his bearded face, while his fingers press into her thigh so realistically that the stone seems to be soft flesh. The three-headed dog Cerberus stands at their feet.

**Apollo and Daphne**
Another Borghese marble showing the moment the nymph Daphne, fleeing Apollo, turns into a laurel tree: leaves and branches sprout from her fingers and bark grows up her legs. Bernini's assistant Giuliano Finelli helped carve the delicate leaves and other details.

**Truth Unveiled by Time**
An unfinished allegorical sculpture of a nude young woman (Truth) holding a radiant sun and resting her foot on a globe. Bernini planned a figure of Time pulling a drape off her but never carved it. He began it as a personal statement after he was criticized when the bell towers he designed for St. Peter's Basilica developed cracks and were torn down.

**David**
Bernini's Borghese David shows the hero in the middle of action, twisting his body and biting his lip as he swings his sling at a Goliath who is imagined to be behind the viewer. A harp lies at his feet. It is often contrasted with Michelangelo's calm, standing David.

**Baldacchino of St. Peter's**
A huge bronze canopy with twisted Solomonic columns over the high altar of St. Peter's Basilica, commissioned by Pope Urban VIII Barberini. It stands beneath Michelangelo's dome and marks the place of St. Peter's tomb. Barberini bees appear on it.

**Blessed Ludovica Albertoni**
A late sculpture in the church of San Francesco a Ripa in Rome's Trastevere district. The dying mystic Ludovica Albertoni lies on a mattress above a red marble sarcophagus, clutching her breast, with cherub heads above her. A painting by Bernini's follower Baciccio hangs behind it.

**Bust of Costanza Bonarelli**
An informal, intimate marble portrait of Bernini's mistress, with lips parted and her chemise open. When Bernini discovered she was having an affair with his brother Luigi, he had a servant slash her face.

**Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius**
An early Borghese group showing the Trojan hero Aeneas, wearing a lion skin, carrying his old father Anchises on his shoulders as they flee burning Troy. Anchises holds the statues of the household gods (penates), and the young Ascanius carries the sacred fire of the hearth.

**Tomb of Pope Alexander VII**
A tomb in St. Peter's Basilica where a gilded bronze skeleton of Death lifts an hourglass from under a marble shroud of red jasper below the kneeling pope. Among the allegorical figures, Truth rests her foot on England on a globe, a reference to the pope's opposition to Anglicanism. Bernini also made the earlier tomb of Urban VIII.

**Cathedra Petri (Chair of St. Peter)**
A gilded bronze reliquary in the apse of St. Peter's that encases a wooden chair believed to have been used by St. Peter. Above it, an oval window of yellow alabaster shows the dove of the Holy Spirit surrounded by golden rays.

**Fountains for the Barberini: Triton Fountain and Fountain of the Bees**
Two Roman fountains made for Urban VIII's Barberini family, whose emblem is the bee. In the Triton Fountain, the sea god kneels on a shell and blows water through a conch, while the smaller Fountain of the Bees shows three bees on a large open seashell and was meant to provide water for people and horses.
